All four years of it.

A student template for the Math Ed ePortfolio: what you add each year, and the habits that turn a folder of files into ongoing learning.

Template · First-year math education majors

Selection. Reflection. Connection.

Definition 1.1 (ePortfolio). A curated collection of student-created work — for learning, assessment, and showcase — with reflection on each artifact and on the connections between them.

Corollary (Math Ed Portfolio). The same thing, organized around what a beginning mathematics teacher needs to be able to do. Without reflection it is a repository. With it, it is the argument, with evidence, that you are ready for your own classroom.

What makes it a learning portfolioSlide 02

A repository stores work. A learning portfolio returns to it.

Four features separate an ePortfolio that supports ongoing learning from a website with files on it. Every year of this template is built around them.

Return & revise

Nothing is written once. The philosophy statement, goals, and key reflections get a new dated version every cycle — and the old versions stay visible so growth is something you can point to.

Reflection tied to artifacts

Every reflection links to a specific artifact and quotes or points at a specific place in it. Claims without evidence don't go in.

Feedback that gets a response

Mentor, cooperating teacher, and peer feedback is logged — and each entry gets a short reply from the student: what changed, or why it didn't.

Connection across contexts

Prompts ask how this is like, and not like, what came before: another course, a placement, the student's own schooling. That is where transfer happens.

MILE alignmentSlide 03

Every MILE requirement is met by a math ed artifact

MILE asks for About Me, one artifact + reflection from Advanced Writing and from each of three Applied Skills Courses, one from Capstone, and a concluding reflection — all in the Google Site shell from UNV 101, submitted to MILO in Capstone. The math ed portfolio supplies each one.

The four-year arcSlide 04

Built in step with the program, not on top of it

Two to three artifacts a year. The MILE portfolio shell you create in UNV 101 is the same Google Site; the math ed pages are added alongside it.

Year 1

Begin the record

Site shell · baseline letter · philosophy v1 · one piece of your own mathematics

Year 2

Observation notes · first lesson plan · philosophy v2 · goal check-in

Year 3

Teach and analyze

Second lesson plan · student-work analysis · assessment you designed · feedback log

Student teaching & capstone

Classroom video with commentary · philosophy v4 · concluding reflection · MILE submission

Every year:reread last year's letter to your future self · write the next one · new dated philosophy version · goal check-in with your mentor · reply to every piece of logged feedback
Year 1 of 4Slide 05

Begin the record

Most of Year 1 is setting a baseline you will come back to. It feels small now; it is the most-referenced material in the whole portfolio.

What you add

  • Portfolio shell (MILE) Create your Google Site in UNV 101 — this is the MILE shell. Write the About Me page and add a Math Ed section with placeholder pages for each year.
  • Letter to your future self Who are you, and who do you want to become as a math teacher? What are you worried about? What do you want to learn here?
  • Teaching philosophy v1 One page. It will be wrong in interesting ways, which is the point of keeping it.
  • One piece of your own mathematics (MILE · ASC) A proof or exploration from a first-year course, with a note on what was hard. If the course is a Quantitative Reasoning ASC, this is your MILE artifact for it.

What keeps learning going

  • Dated versions Name files and pages with the semester (philosophy-F26). Never overwrite; add.
  • Goals you can check Three concrete goals at the end of the letter. Year 2 opens by grading them.
  • A first mentor conversation Meet your faculty mentor; they get share access to the site — and a promise you'll remove them when you graduate.
  • Muddiest point One sentence: what about teaching math is least clear to you right now?
Reflection promptWhat do you already believe about how people learn mathematics — and where did that belief come from?
Year 2 of 4Slide 06

First classroom evidence

Early field experience and the first methods course produce the first artifacts from real classrooms. Year 2 is where the connection prompts start doing work.

What you add

  • Observation notes From early field experience: what you saw, and one moment you'd have handled differently.
  • First lesson plan (MILE · ASC) From a methods course, with standards alignment and anticipated student responses. If the course is an Oral Communication or Teamwork ASC, submit it with its reflection as the MILE artifact.
  • Teaching philosophy v2 Rewritten, not edited. Then a short note: what changed since v1, and what caused it.
  • Goal check-in Reread the Year 1 letter. Score each goal. Write the Year 2 letter.

What keeps learning going

  • Like / not like For the lesson plan: how is planning a lesson like, and not like, solving a problem set? Like, and not like, being a student in that lesson?
  • Answer the muddiest point Return to last year's question. Is it clearer? What made it clearer?
  • Feedback log begins Methods instructor feedback on the lesson plan goes in — with your reply: what you'd change and why.
  • Peer read Trade portfolios with a classmate; each leaves one comment the other must answer.
Reflection promptPoint to one line in your lesson plan that you would not have written a year ago. What do you know now?
Year 3 of 4Slide 07

Teach and analyze

Placements give you student thinking to work with. Year 3 shifts the portfolio from what you planned to what students actually did.

What you add

  • Second lesson plan Different grade band or strand than the first — say, middle-school proportional reasoning after a high-school proof lesson.
  • Analysis of student work Real (anonymized) responses to a task you gave, sorted by strategy and misconception, with what you'd do next.
  • Assessment you designed A quiz, task, or rubric, plus results and what they told you.
  • Teaching philosophy v3 (MILE · Advanced Writing) Now with evidence: each claim links to an artifact. This is the Advanced Writing artifact for MILE, reflection included.

What keeps learning going

  • Lesson wrapper After teaching: how did you prepare, where did students struggle, what will you do differently next time? Modeled on exam wrappers.
  • Compare plan to plan Set the Year 2 and Year 3 lesson plans side by side. Name three differences and what they show.
  • Feedback with response Cooperating teacher and supervisor observations are logged; each gets a reply within a week.
  • Regulatory checklist Before a lesson: what is the task, my goal, my plan? After: did it work, what didn't, what next?
Reflection promptFind a student response that surprised you. What did the student understand that your plan didn't anticipate?
Year 4 of 4Slide 08

Student teaching & capstone

The last year turns the record into an argument. The capstone reflection is the MILE requirement; the portfolio presentation is the program's.

What you add

  • Classroom video with commentary (MILE · Capstone) 10–15 minutes of you teaching, with time-stamped notes on the questions you asked and the decisions you made. The Capstone artifact for MILE.
  • Teaching philosophy v4 Final version, presented beside v1. The distance between them is the evidence.
  • Growth record Every logged piece of feedback with its response, and what you did about it.
  • Concluding reflection (MILE) The MILE concluding reflection on the whole experience, plus a program reflection that walks a reader through the math ed pages. Submit the site link through MILO's form for graduation credit.

What keeps learning going

  • Integration reflection Referencing specific artifacts across all four years: what can you do now that you couldn't? How does this prepare you for your first classroom?
  • Reread every letter Four letters to your future self, in order. Write the fifth: to yourself at the end of your first year teaching.
  • Portfolio presentation Present to faculty and peers. Then reply to their feedback in the growth record — the last entry.
  • Hand-off Submit the link via the MILO form in Capstone. Remove instructors' access — MILO recommends sharing, not publishing. The site is yours for the job search and beyond.
Reflection promptChoose one artifact from each year. Together, what story do they tell about how you learned to teach mathematics?
The reflection cycleSlide 09

Every artifact gets a reflection — and the reflection points at the artifact

Four prompt families, drawn from the Miami ePortfolios Working Group. Use one or more per artifact; require a link or a quotation from the artifact in every answer.

Process

Describe the work. What surprised or challenged you? What would you do differently, and why? What tools and resources did you use, and how did they help or hinder?

Outcomes

How did this artifact help you learn X? Point to the place in it where you demonstrate your ability to do Y.

Integration

How does this connect to earlier courses, placements, or your own schooling? How does it prepare you for what you hope to do next?

Development

How have you grown as a mathematics teacher since the last version? Point to iterations to show it.

What the mentor does with it

Reflection that nobody responds to stops happening. Each reflection gets a short reply from the faculty mentor within two weeks — one question, one observation — and the student answers it. The exchange stays on the page.

Features that recur every yearSlide 10

The same five moves, four times

Ongoing learning comes from repetition with variation. These are the pages a student returns to each year; the grid shows how each one deepens.

Artifact page templateSlide 11

One page, the same shape every time

Each artifact in the Google Site follows this layout, so a reader — or the student in Year 4 — can find the reflection and the feedback without hunting.

Lesson Plan · Proportional Reasoning, Grade 7F27 · Methods I

Artifact
Embedded PDF or Doc. Standards, objectives, anticipated responses.
Context
Course, placement, grade band, what came just before and after.
Reflection
Process · Outcomes · Integration · Development — with links to specific parts of the artifact.
Feedback & reply
Instructor / mentor comment, dated. Student reply, dated.
Connections
Links to the earlier artifact this builds on, and the philosophy version it informs.
Next step
One sentence: what this artifact says you should try next.

Using this templateSlide 12

What the program needs to build, in order of urgency

Start with the smallest piece inside your own locus of control. Everything below can be piloted in one methods section before it's a program requirement.

1

Artifact page template & instructions

One Google Sites page students copy. Include the six section headings and the reflection prompt families.

2

Year 1 letter & philosophy prompts

Baseline reflections assigned in UNV 101 or the first math ed course. These must exist before anything else can be revisited.

3

Reflection rubric

Shared by all mentors. Two criteria carry most of the weight: is the claim tied to a specific place in the artifact, and does it connect to prior work?

4

Feedback-reply norm

A two-week reply window for mentors, and a one-week reply window for students. Written down, so it happens.

5

Year 4 presentation format

Twenty minutes, four artifacts, one per year. Announce it in Year 1 so students select with it in mind.

6

ASC designations

Ask which math and education courses will be designated Applied Skills Courses, so the artifact map above matches real course numbers. MILO's reflection-prompt bank and Howe Center workshops cover the rest.

Sources: Miami ePortfolios Working Group, F'26 (Wardle, Olejnik, Boddy, Bapst) · Perkins & Salomon on transfer · Schraw (1998) regulatory checklists · Lovett (2016) exam wrappers · Tanner (2012)
